clue.text: The last to get a shift shows furtive manner

indicators.note: to shift something is to move it about, so these letters are moved into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, seven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: The newest worker is handed the shift nobody wants, and their sly behaviour shows it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last' reads like a person at the back of a queue, but it is just seven letters, and 'shift' is the signal to move them.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealth is secret, quiet behaviour meant to avoid notice, which is exactly a sly or sneaky way of acting.

clue.text: Revolutionary is leading element close to workers' protests

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the word that follows is turned back to front

parts.note: taken as written before being turned round
tin is a chemical element

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its final letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A firebrand leads the way in the workers' demonstrations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading' only says the turned-round piece goes before the metal. 'Revolutionary' looks like the firebrand of the surface, but it just flips the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A sit-in is a form of demonstration where people occupy a building and refuse to leave, so sit-ins are protests.

clue.text: Fighter breaking a rule badly gets long reprimand

indicators.note: to break into something is to get inside it, so one piece goes inside the other
done badly means done wrong, so the letters come out in the wrong order

parts.note: taken as written, five letters to rearrange
F labels fighter aircraft, as in the F-16

explanation.surface: A boxer who fouls his opponent is given a long telling-off by the referee.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged EARUL is split by F: EAR + F + UL makes EARFUL. 'Fighter' looks like a boxer, but in crosswords F stands for a fighter plane.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting an earful is an idiom for being scolded at length, so the word names a lengthy telling-off.

clue.text: Scientific site over year favoured this when shorn of international networks

indicators.note: something shorn has had part cut away, so a letter is clipped out

parts.note: a lab is where scientists work
YR is the standard abbreviation for year
something in favour or fashionable is said to be in
taken as written before losing a letter
I is the abbreviation for international

explanation.surface: A laboratory once popular with researchers lost out when cut off from its overseas connections.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'over' puts LAB above YR. THIS without I leaves THS, and LAB + YR + IN + THS spells LABYRINTHS.
explanation.definitionFit: A labyrinth is a maze of tangled passages or interconnected paths, so labyrinths are complicated networks.

clue.text: Sweltering Celt taking off jacket in tourist accommodation

parts.note: sweltering means very hot

indicators.note: a jacket is the outer layer, so removing it strips the first and last letters and keeps the inside

parts.note: the word with its outer letters removed

explanation.surface: A Scot or Irishman, overheated, strips off his coat in a holiday hotel room.
explanation.walkthrough: The jacket is the outside letters of 'Celt', so only its middle EL survives.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotel is a building offering rooms and meals to travellers and holidaymakers who pay to stay.

clue.text: Idiot has to stop detaining fine all-female group

indicators.note: to detain is to hold someone, so one piece holds the others inside it

parts.note: to halt is to stop
F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
the WI is the Women's Institute, a British women's organisation

explanation.surface: A fool is ordered to stop holding up a decent women's club.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute is a British community organisation for women, known for jam and cake stalls. HAL(F WI)T: HALT holds F and WI.
explanation.definitionFit: A halfwit is an insulting word for a stupid or foolish person, so it is a synonym of the noun.

clue.text: Ambassador with attitude about India is dithering

parts.note: HE stands for His or Her Excellency, the title of an ambassador

indicators.note: about here means surrounding, so one piece goes round another

parts.note: a stance is an attitude or position
India is I in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A diplomat's stance on India is wavering.
explanation.walkthrough: HE is a crossword convention for an ambassador, from the title His Excellency. STANCE wraps I to give S(I)TANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Hesitance is uncertainty that stops you acting quickly, which is the same as indecisive wavering or dithering.

clue.text: See paper in elevated room

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see
the FT is the Financial Times newspaper

explanation.surface: Go and look at the newspaper up in the attic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lo and behold' keeps the old exclamation LO alive; 'paper' as a newspaper is a common hint for FT, the Financial Times.
explanation.definitionFit: A loft is the space or room under the roof of a building, reached by going upstairs.

clue.text: Drive shown by old boy in Hertfordshire town producing theatrical costumes

indicators.note: being in a place means being surrounded by it, so the pieces go inside

parts.note: Ware is a market town in Hertfordshire, England
DR is the street abbreviation for Drive
OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

explanation.surface: A former pupil shows his determination by putting on plays in a small English town.
explanation.walkthrough: Ware is a small town north of London; it wraps DR and OB to make WAR(DR OB)E. 'Drive' looks like ambition but is a street abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A theatre's wardrobe is its stock of stage clothes and the department that looks after them.

clue.text: Old comic afterwards trimmed and in fine fettle

indicators.note: trimming cuts a little off the end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: then means afterwards
dandy is an informal adjective for fine or excellent

explanation.surface: A veteran comedian, once he has had a haircut, looks in excellent shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old comic' wants to be a retired comedian, but it is a magazine. THEN loses its last letter to give THE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dandy was a long-running British children's comic magazine, which ended in print in 2012.

clue.text: Pulse starts to trouble husband resting on bed

indicators.note: the start of each word is its first letter, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: the first letter of each of the five words

explanation.surface: A heartbeat begins to bother a man lying in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letters of five words in a row spell the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A throb is a strong regular beat, like that of the heart, so it is a synonym of pulse.

clue.text: Stock fare prepared for working party

indicators.note: food that is prepared has been worked over, so the letters are remade into something new

parts.note: taken as written, nine letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Standard food is laid on for a group of workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock fare' reads like soup or basic catering, but it is only the letters to be reworked.
explanation.definitionFit: A task force is a group set up to deal with a particular job, which is what a working party is.

clue.text: Grey Geneva, maybe, lacking a leader? It's a Swiss hallmark

indicators.note: the leader is whoever goes in front, so losing it removes the first letter

parts.note: grey is a neutral colour
Geneva is an example of a city, as 'maybe' signals

explanation.surface: A dull, leaderless Geneva could be the trademark of Switzerland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' tells you Geneva stands for the class it belongs to, CITY, which then drops its first letter to give ITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Switzerland is famous for staying out of wars and alliances, so not taking sides is a defining Swiss trait.

clue.text: Stadium lacking in new locality

indicators.note: lacking something means being without it, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: an arena is a stadium
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A neighbourhood that has no new sports ground.
explanation.walkthrough: ARENA minus its N leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A locality is a district or neighbourhood, and area is the everyday word for such a region.

clue.text: Suspect cleaner hid hanging feature?

indicators.note: something suspect is dodgy and not to be trusted as it stands, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ten letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: In a whodunit, the cleaner under suspicion concealed something connected with an execution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' looks like a noun for the cleaner, but it is an adjective telling you to rearrange the letters. The question mark flags that 'hanging' is not about the gallows.
explanation.definitionFit: A chandelier is an ornamental light fitting that hangs from the ceiling, a decorative suspended feature of a room.

clue.text: Stop at an early stage trouble behind input

indicators.note: to trouble something is to disturb it, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, eleven letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Halt a project early because the contributions are running late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trouble' looks like a noun in the surface but works as a verb that churns the following two words.
explanation.definitionFit: To nip something in the bud is an idiom from gardening meaning to halt it before it can develop.

clue.text: Activity of those out to deter others?

definitions.text: Activity of those out to deter others?

parts.words: Activity of those out to deter others?
parts.note: surface reading: people whose aim is to discourage others from something
setter's reading: out means on strike, and strikers stand at the gates trying to stop colleagues going in to work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Out' reads as 'intent on', but in industrial language workers who are out are on strike.
explanation.definitionFit: Strikers gather outside a workplace to persuade other workers not to cross the line and go in, which is a picket.

clue.text: Obstruct one riding horse

parts.note: to stall is to hold up or obstruct
I is the Roman numeral one
riding a horse means being on it

explanation.surface: Block the way of somebody on horseback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One riding' looks like a rider, but it is two pieces: I for one and ON for riding.
explanation.definitionFit: A stallion is an adult male horse that has not been castrated, so it is one kind of horse.

clue.text: Problem in turn with tiros cooking Mexican food

indicators.note: turning something round brings its end to the front, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: a rub is a difficulty, as in 'there's the rub'

indicators.note: cooking transforms ingredients, so these letters are worked into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written; tiros are beginners

explanation.surface: There is trouble when novices take their turn in the kitchen making Mexican dishes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There's the rub', from Hamlet, keeps the old sense of a snag alive. A tiro (or tyro) is a beginner.
explanation.definitionFit: Burritos are tortillas wrapped round a filling of meat or beans, a well-known dish from Mexican cuisine.

clue.text: Suggestion to conceal display device

parts.note: a touch is a slight hint or suggestion, as in a touch of irony
to screen is to hide from view

explanation.surface: Someone proposes hiding a monitor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suggestion' is a noun for a trace, not a proposal: a touch of salt is a suggestion of it.
explanation.definitionFit: A touch screen is a panel that both shows images and responds to fingers, so it is a kind of display device.

clue.text: Appalled by Henry, when getting into a sports car

indicators.note: to get into something is to go inside it, so one piece ends up within another

parts.note: taken as written
GT, gran turismo, labels a fast touring sports car
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
as can mean when, as in 'as I arrived'

explanation.surface: Someone is horrified to see Henry climbing into a sports car.
explanation.walkthrough: Henry looks like a person but is the henry, the physics unit of inductance, written H. GT, for gran turismo, is a common crossword sports car.
explanation.definitionFit: Aghast means filled with horror or shock, so it is a direct synonym of the adjective appalled.

clue.text: Decorative covering never altered around front of exhibits

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so one piece wraps round another
something altered has been changed, so these letters are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, five letters to rearrange

indicators.note: the front of a word is where it begins, so its first letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: An ornamental layer has been left unchanged around the front of the display pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Never altered' sounds like something kept unchanged, but 'altered' tells you to rearrange the letters, which then go round E.
explanation.definitionFit: A veneer is a thin attractive layer of wood or other material glued over a cheaper surface to make it look better.

clue.text: Liberal Scottish musician provides attraction

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for Liberal
Midge Ure is a Scottish singer and guitarist, frontman of Ultravox

explanation.surface: A left-leaning Scottish performer is a real draw.
explanation.walkthrough: Midge Ure, the Scottish musician behind Ultravox and co-organiser of Band Aid, supplies the last three letters after L for Liberal.
explanation.definitionFit: A lure is something that tempts or draws people in, which is what an attraction does.

clue.text: Knowledgeable solicitor, say, on a roll finally with a great score in golf

parts.note: in cricket the on side of the field is also called the leg side
taken as written

indicators.note: finally points at the end of a word, so only its last letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
an eagle is two strokes under par on a golf hole

explanation.surface: A clever lawyer on a winning streak caps it with a superb golf score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On a roll' looks like a set phrase but splits apart: in cricket the on side is the leg side, giving LEG. 'Say' marks the solicitor as just one example of the type.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal eagle is an informal term for a sharp, able lawyer, and a well-informed solicitor is an example.

clue.text: Prank by one opposing Conservative

parts.note: someone anti something is opposed to it
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: A practical joke played by a political opponent of the Tories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One opposing Conservative' reads as a single political rival, but it splits into ANTI and C.
explanation.definitionFit: An antic is a silly or playful act, usually in the plural, so it is close in meaning to a prank or caper.

clue.text: Some superior feed for pond fish

indicators.note: some means only a part, so the letters come from inside the words that follow

parts.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Better-quality food for the fish in a garden pond.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the gap between the two words. It is a less common word, so the crossing letters help.
explanation.definitionFit: The orfe, or ide, is a freshwater fish often kept in its golden form in ornamental ponds.

clue.text: Ban dire criminal entering international court

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: INT is the abbreviation for international
CT is the abbreviation for court

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so these letters are twisted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, four letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A dreadful offender appearing before a world tribunal is barred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal' looks like a noun for the offender, but it is an adjective telling you to rearrange the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: An interdict is a formal prohibition, especially a court order or church decree forbidding something, so it is a ban.

clue.text: This writer's mature portrayal

parts.note: the writer of the clue refers to themself as I, and 'writer's' is short for 'writer is', so I am becomes I'M
to mature is to age

explanation.surface: The author's grown-up depiction of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s reads as possessive, but it is 'is': this writer is gives I'M. 'Mature' is a verb, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a picture or likeness of something, and a portrayal is a representation in words or art.

clue.text: Bread in store for later needs?

definitions.text: Bread in store for later needs?

parts.note: surface reading: a loaf kept in the larder for future meals
setter's reading: bread is slang for money, so this is cash put aside for later life

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread' wants to be a loaf in the cupboard, but it is old slang for money; the question mark flags the trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A sum of savings set aside for the future, for retirement or emergencies, is called by this idiom.

clue.text: Conservator has short form essentially about introduction to antiquities

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: curt means short or abrupt in manner

indicators.note: an introduction comes first, so the opening letter of the next word is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

indicators.note: the essence of something is at its heart, so the middle letters are kept

parts.note: the inner letters of the word

explanation.surface: A museum conservator fills in a brief form about an antiques collection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like it describes the form, but it is a word for abrupt that wraps round the first letter of 'antiquities'.
explanation.definitionFit: A curator looks after the collection of a museum or gallery, preserving its objects, so the job overlaps with a conservator's.
